text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

In its monthly Bulletin, the Reserve Bank has warned that the ACTU's "living wage" claim, which would add 1.6 percent to the economy-wide wages bill, would blow out the inflation rate by pushing aggregate wages growth well over five percent a year because of the wage claim's flow-on effects for workers covered by enterprise agreements and informal wage deals. Page 1.

Just a week after Prime Minister John Howard ruled out further major fiscal savings for the time being, the Reserve Bank of Australia has strongly emphasised the importance of tighter budget policy and warned that the recent improvement in the deficit "will need to be sustained in the medium term". Page 1.

In an outsourcing deal brokered by the AMP Society and Andersen Consulting described as a world first, AMP has handed the reigns of its A$750 million technology budget for the next five years to Andersen - a move which will mean AMP remains the owner of the IT assets and staff, but the IT operations will be managed, and partly staffed, by Andersen consultants. Page 3.

According to the Green Paper, a government planning paper produced by industry groups, environmental organisations and the federal government to be released today, the price of energy should increase to include the full cost to society of pollution caused by its production and use. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Reserve Bank's monthly Bulletin, released yesterday, stepped up the bank's attack on the ACTU living wage, saying adoption of the first stage of the ACTU's claim would boost total wages by two percent - a move which the Reserve says would threaten recent interest rate cuts and employment growth. Page 1.

In the New South Wales Supreme Court yesterday, Justice Hubert Bell awarded 32-year-old Kathryn Curtin A$524,000 in damages after her cancer condition went undiagnosed for almost two years despite consulting doctors 17 times before the cancer was found and she was told she was too young to have a mammogram. Page 1.

Following a meeting of arts ministers at the Cultural Ministers Council, the first to be held since the federal election, the state symphony orchestras are to be corporatised and fully separated from the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, with the A$32 million provided through the ABC for the orchestras to be fully transferred and indexed. Page 3.

The appointment of secretary of the federal Department of Employment, Education, Training and Youth Affairs, Sandy Hollway to the Sydney Olympics organising committee yesterday triggered a political row, with New South Wales Opposition spokesman on the Olympics Ian Armstrong saying the committee was in danger of becoming a "who's who of the Labor Party". Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In a move which will revolutionise health insurance in Australia, the country's largest health lobby group, the Australian Health Insurance Association, has revealed that, due to rising costs and falling membership of health funds, privately insured patinets will face severe restrictions on their choice of hospitals. Page 1.

News Corp chairman Rupert Murdoch, ruling himself out of contention to assume control of John Fairfax, said yesterday that Fairfax's new majority shareholder Brierley Investments was a market opportunist and predicted either Kerry Packer or Irish media owner Tony O'Reilly may end up owning the newspaper group. He also criticised Prime Minister John Howard for "outdated" views on media ownership. Page 1.

Kate Curtin, a young Sydney woman who is dying of cancer, has been awarded more than A$500,000 damages after successfully suing her general practitioner Louise Holliday and endocrinologist Phillip Bligh, who were both found to be negligent after advising Curtin she was too young to need a mammogram. Page 1.

A new study by Macquarie University School of Earth Sciences lecturer Paul Beggs, who surveyed 3,000 children aged five to nine in the Willoughby, Camden and Leichardt local government areas, has found children living in older homes with the highest reported incidence of mould and the biggest proportion of dust mites in their beds have a lower incidence of asthma than some children living in environments with fewer allergens. Page 3.
THE AGE

Speaking in Tokyo, News Corp chairman Rupert Murdoch yesterday said Brierley Investments was not a serious player and accused the New Zealand firm of being a market opportunist in its purchase of 25 percent of Fairfax. Murdoch predicted that the eventual owner of Fairfax could be Kerry Packer or Irish media owner Tony O'Reilly. Page A1.

Victorian Tertiary Education Minister Phil Honeywood said yesterday multi-million dollar bids by the state's universities to expand into Malaysia could be under threat following reports of alleged racial abuse of a Malaysian student in Melbourne. He said the reports had come at a crucial time, with two universities poised to win lucrative contracts to set up campuses in Malaysia. Page A1.

Fiona McLeod, who was appointed Victoria's electricity ombudsman in May, has criticised customer service standards in the privatised power industry, and has ordered United Energy to pay thousands of dollars to customers affected by power surges. In her fist report, released yesterday, McLeod revealed her office had received a further 376 complaints against electricity companies in its first six months. Page A1.

According to a Federal Office of Road Safety study which compared nations in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, Victoria is the second safest place to drive in the world, with 1.3 deaths for every 10,000 cars. Overall, Australia finished fourth behind Switzerland, Norway and Sweden. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
